extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria governing professional conduct, misconduct findings, and sanctions for practitioners practicing before the United States Patent and Trademark Office. Includes duties (candor, inquiry, communication), definitions of neglect/misconduct, evidentiary and sanctioning factors, and relevant regulatory citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and on-sale bars to patentability (35 U.S.C. § 102(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability of an invention is barred as a matter of law if the invention is described in a written publication more than one year before filing a patent application, or if the invention is placed on sale in the United States more than one year before filing. An electronic publication on the internet is considered a written publication for purposes of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The loss of patentability is known as the 'publication bar' and the 'on sale bar.' See MPEP § 2128 for internet publications. A practitioner publishing a client's invention on the internet and offering it for sale more than 12 months before the client's application is filed is dealing with information material to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and disclosure of material information (37 C.F.R. § 1.56(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner prosecuting a client's application before the Office has the duty of candor and good faith in dealing with the Office, including a duty to disclose to the Office all information known to that individual to be material to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information such as an attorney's publication of a client's invention on the internet and offering it for sale (which can trigger the publication/on-sale bars) is material and must be disclosed. Failure to disclose material information may constitute unethical conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner certification on papers — truthfulness and reasonable inquiry (37 C.F.R. § 10.18(b)/(11.18))
rubrics_metrics.description: By presenting a paper to the Office (signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating), a practitioner certifies that statements of personal knowledge are true, statements on information and belief are believed to be true, and that, after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, (i) the paper is not presented for any improper purpose and (ii) the claims and other legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The certificate requires a substantive pre-filing inquiry where appropriate; merely assuming facts or not checking obvious sources (e.g., the practitioner's own website where the invention may have been published) is insufficient. Violations subject practitioner to disciplinary action (see 37 C.F.R. § 10.18(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on signing a paper in violation of § 10.18 (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15))
rubrics_metrics.description: Signing a paper filed in the Office in violation of the provisions of § 10.18 is a specific violation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15)) and constitutes misconduct under § 10.23(a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner certifies, via signature, that a reasonable inquiry was performed but did not actually undertake such an inquiry (for example, failed to check known public disclosures), that signature violates § 10.18 and triggers disciplinary provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct. Any violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c) constitutes a violation of § 10.23(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 10.23(a) itself does not require proof of intent; violations of enumerated subsection provisions (e.g., signing in violation of § 10.18, failing to communicate with a client) satisfy this prohibition. The regulation is broad and includes many specific proscribed acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not neglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect is defined as the omission of proper attention to a person or thing (inadvertent, negligent, or willful). Lack of diligence can range from virtual abandonment to procrastination, and should be examined along a temporal continuum rather than as isolated events. Examples: failure to file a patent application timely, failing to maintain awareness of case status, failing to respond to Office actions, misplacing files, or having nonfunctional docketing/tickler systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate to client about correspondence having significant effect (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner misconduct includes failing to inform a client of correspondence from the Office having a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to advise a client of an Office Action or Notice of Abandonment that affects their patent rights is a violation; such failures also may be an aggravating factor in sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to maintain functional office management and docketing systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are expected to maintain adequate and functional systems (tickler/docketing systems and file organization) to monitor deadlines and case status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A manual, error-prone filing system, missing backups, or nonfunctional 'tickler' systems that create an 'ever-present threat' of forgetfulness expose clients to harm and support findings of neglect. Reasonable and readily available precautions should be taken; failure to do so is evidence of negligent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of practitioner's state of mind for sanctioning (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing exclusion or suspension, the Director/ALJ must consider whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some disciplinary provisions do not require intent, the practitioner's mental state (intentional vs. negligent) is relevant to the severity of sanction (intentional misconduct suggests harsher sanction; negligent misconduct may suggest less punitive sanction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of actual or potential injury caused by misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctioning decisions must consider the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of the client's opportunity to obtain a patent and exploit an invention is a serious deprivation even if monetary damages are not easily quantified; such harm justifies a sanction of at least moderate severity depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of aggravating and mitigating factors in determining sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director/ALJ must consider aggravating and mitigating factors when imposing suspension or exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors include prior disciplinary history, recalcitrance after warnings, multiple instances of similar misconduct. Mitigating factors can include extensive prior successful practice, restitution/refund of fees (may be neutral if motivation ambiguous), and other contextual information. ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions (e.g., §9.22) are routinely consulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for disciplinary findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary findings by the ALJ/USPTO are evaluated under a heightened evidentiary standard (referenced in the record as 'clear and convincing evidence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts of misconduct are typically proven on the record to the ALJ by clear and convincing evidence; the Director reviews the ALJ record and may affirm, modify, or remand (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.55(f), 11.56(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and evaluation of neglect (case-law and dictionary guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect includes omission of proper attention to a matter, failing to act or act diligently; it is evaluated by reference to precedent and legal definitions (e.g., Black's Law Dictionary, In re Magar, In re Alexander).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect is assessed in the 'broader context of the representation' focusing on knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation. A single missed task may be part of a broader pattern of neglect when viewed temporally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on presenting papers for improper purpose or frivolous legal contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not present papers for improper purposes and must ensure claims and legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for law change (37 C.F.R. § 10.18(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting claims lacking any legal basis or without reasonable grounds for a nonfrivolous argument violates certification obligations. The certification requirement demands a reasonable factual and legal inquiry prior to filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural right to de novo review on appeal and related procedural rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.55(f), 11.56(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: On appeal from an ALJ's initial decision, the USPTO Director may conduct a de novo review of the factual record and may affirm, reverse, or modify the initial decision, or remand the matter for further proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals must be filed within 30 days; requests for reconsideration have specific timing and service requirements. The Director's review uses the record before the ALJ, and sanctions must be explained in light of § 11.54(b) factors.
